Circumstances leading to this rule are as follows: Opposite party decree holder instituted other suit No. 45 of 1965 in the Court of Munsif, Roazan for specific performance of contract for sale and ultimately obtained a decree for Rs. 1000/- for money that was advanced by him with costs On 31.1.66, the opposite party decree holder also obtained a decree for Rs. 287.50 in the Court of No. 1 Haldia Union Council which he put into execution as well in other execution case No. 48 of 1967 in the aforesaid Court of the learned Munsif. Thereafter he put his decree for Rs. 1000/- obtained in other suit No. 45 of 1965, being execution case No. 8 of 1967, and attached some of the property of the petitioner-judgment debtor. Subsequently the decree holder agreed to accept Rs. 1000/- as full satisfaction of the debt in both the aforesaid two execution cases and the petitioner paid Rs. 750/- in cash to the decree holder who also granted a receipt for it, and it was settled that if the balance of the money be paid within one month then the decree holder would not proceed with the execution. A compromise to that affect was effected in presence of witnesses  The petitioner  it is alleged could not pay the balance of Rs. 250/- in time. The decree holder again proceeded with execution of both the cases for the entire decretal amount without adjusting Rs. 750/- paid by the petitioner. Thereafter the petitioner filed an application under section 47 C. P. C. alleging the aforesaid talk of compromise and the -payment of Rs. 750/- and a Misc. Case No. 53 of 1967 as stated above was started which was ultimately fixed for hearing on 24.6.67 but due to some illness the petitioner could not attend the court on that date and the case was dismissed for default. The petitioner then filed the present application on 20. 7. 67 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the said Misc. Case which was opposed by a decree holder opposite party. 

 4. In 7 D.L.R. 231, Mr. Tabibar Rahman Talukder Vs Sudhir Numer Saba Chowdhury the question for determination was whether an order dismissing an objection that the value stated in the sale proclamation was too low and that it was not properly drawn up and published is open to appeal as an order under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 5. In 8 D.L.R. 147, Benoyendra Nath Roy Choudury and others Vs. Jaday Chandra Roy Choudury, the judgment debtor appellants filed a Misc. Case under section 47 C. P. C. objecting to the executing of decree supported by respondent on the ground, inter alia, that it was barred under section 69 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and that no notice under Order 21 rule 66 C. P. C. for determination of the valuation of the mortgage property was served. The Misc. Case came up for hearing but as neither party took any step it was dismissed for default. This was restored on an application under section 151 C. P. C. and a date was fixed for peremptory hearing and on that date again the appellants did not take any step, although the decree holder was present. The Misc. case was again dismissed for default and on the same day again an application for setting aside the dismissal for default was filed which was subsequently rejected after hearing both the parties. Thereafter the appellants-judgment-debtor filed another application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the same ground as stated in the earlier application under section 47 C. P. C. which was rejected by the court against which the appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. It was observed by the Division Bench of the High Court as follows: 

 11.The corresponding section of the former Code, namely, section 647 of the Code of 1877 as it originally stood and on which their lordships of the Privy Council made the observation as stated above ran as follows : 

 13. The attention of their lords lips of Privy Council was called to that amendment introduced by Act VI of 1892 and their lordships  noted the fact that the amendment appears to have been made ill order to avoid the disturbance of practice caused by  the  Allahabad High Court, rulings and having regard to the controversies which have arisen and the difference of opinion between various High Courts their lordships "thought it right to state their opinion that the Act VI of 1892 does nothing more than express the true meaning of Civil Procedure Code." 

 15. It is, therefore, evident that Order lX, rule 9 cannot be said to apply to an execution application which is dismissed for default and far less it would apply to an objection arising out of an execution application and thereafter dismissed for default. The case reported in 8 D.L.R. 147, as stated earlier, has also expressed the opinion that such order of dismissal for default had not the effect of a decree and, as such, is not appealable. Definition of decree under section 2 of sub-section (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure does not include "any order of dismissal for default". It is thus evident that there was no remedy by way of appeal left open to the judgment debtor, dismissing his application under section 47 C.P.C. for default. In these circumstances, his application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the order of dismissal for default cannot be thrown out in limine as not, maintainable and should have been considered on merits.
